title: India Doubled Its Gold Tariff. Smugglers Are Making ₹25 Lakh Per Kilo Bar. NRIs Are Caught in the Middle.
excerpt: The 15 per cent import duty was meant to defend the rupee. Instead it has fuelled a grey-market revival that could hit 100 tons this year — while JP Morgan forecasts $6,000 gold by December.
body:
India just doubled its gold import tariff to 15 per cent. The stated goal was to defend the rupee and narrow the trade deficit. The actual result, within weeks, has been a smuggling revival that could exceed 100 metric tons this year — roughly $14 billion in grey-market gold flowing into the country, depriving the treasury of an estimated $2.65 billion in lost duties and taxes.

For NRIs who buy gold for weddings, festivals, or investment, the new tariff regime has upended every calculation. And with JP Morgan forecasting gold at $6,000 per ounce by year-end, the stakes are only getting higher.

## What Happened

In May, the government more than doubled import duties on gold from 6 per cent to 15 per cent, adding goods and services tax to bring the total levy to 18.45 per cent. The trigger was the Strait of Hormuz crisis: as oil prices spiked above $100 a barrel, India's import bill ballooned, the rupee fell to record lows, and the current account deficit widened dangerously. Curbing gold imports was positioned as fiscal triage.

The problem is that India is the world's second-largest gold market, and demand does not disappear because prices rise — it migrates underground.

## The Smuggling Bonanza



> **"JP Morgan's Greg Shearer describes gold as stuck in "technical no-man's land," trading above its 200-day moving average around $4,340 but capped below the 50-day moving average at $4,730."**


Within weeks of the tariff hike, grey-market gold discounts have widened to more than $200 per ounce below official domestic prices — a margin that makes smuggling irresistible. A single one-kilo gold bar, roughly the size of an iPhone, now offers a smuggling profit of approximately ₹25 lakh ($26,000).

"Even if grey-market operators sell at a 4 per cent discount, they are still making a killing," a Kolkata-based bullion dealer told Reuters. Mumbai-based bullion bankers say legitimate importers cannot offer even a $10 discount, let alone compete with triple-digit grey-market markups. Four dealers interviewed by Reuters estimated illegal imports could exceed 100 tons in 2026.

The legitimate market is feeling the squeeze. India's physically backed gold exchange-traded funds logged their first net monthly outflow in a year in May, as retail investors booked profits following the duty-driven price spike. Jewellers have started restocking, but purchases remain cautious.

## Where Gold Stands Now

Gold is trading at approximately $4,218 per ounce globally, down from its record high of $5,318 in January but still elevated by historical standards. In India, MCX gold futures for August fell more than 3 per cent this past week to around ₹1.50 lakh per 10 grams.

The metal is caught between conflicting forces. On one side: the US-Iran peace deal has eased geopolitical risk premiums, stronger US jobs data has revived rate-hike expectations, and the dollar has firmed — all bearish for gold. On the other: central bank buying remains historically strong (China added reserves for a 19th straight month in May), fiscal deficits are widening globally, and structural inflation concerns persist.

JP Morgan's Greg Shearer describes gold as stuck in "technical no-man's land," trading above its 200-day moving average around $4,340 but capped below the 50-day moving average at $4,730. The bank's full-year target of $6,000 per ounce implies a 42 per cent rally from current levels — driven, it says, by eventual rate cuts and renewed safe-haven demand.

## What NRIs Need to Calculate

The tariff hike creates a practical dilemma for every NRI planning to buy gold in India. Consider the arithmetic: at 15 per cent import duty plus 3 per cent GST, a 10-gram gold purchase in India now carries roughly ₹27,000 in embedded taxes. The same gold bought abroad — in Dubai, Singapore, or the US — carries no such burden, though Indian customs will levy duties if you carry it home.

The duty-free allowance for incoming passengers remains modest: male passengers can bring ₹50,000 worth of gold duty-free, female passengers ₹1 lakh. Anything beyond that attracts the full 18.45 per cent levy. For wedding-season purchases, which routinely run into lakhs, the duty alone can add several lakhs to the total cost.

Digital gold and sovereign gold bonds (SGBs) offer a partial workaround. SGBs carry no GST, offer a 2.5 per cent annual interest rate, and provide tax-free capital gains if held to maturity. But the government has been issuing fewer SGB tranches, and secondary-market premiums have risen.

## The Bigger Picture

India's gold obsession is not irrational. In a country where banking penetration was historically low, gold served as savings, insurance, and collateral. For NRIs, gold remains deeply entwined with family obligations — wedding jewellery, Dhanteras gifts, generational wealth transfer.

The 15 per cent tariff does not diminish that demand. It merely redirects it — from legitimate channels to grey markets, from physical gold to digital alternatives, from India to Dubai. Whether the government can thread the needle between defending the rupee and keeping gold markets functional will determine whether the tariff holds or becomes another chapter in India's long history of gold policy reversals.
nri_angle: NRIs buying gold for weddings or investment now face an 18.45 per cent embedded tax in India — reshaping how and where the diaspora acquires gold.
